FHA.name: FHA (HUD)
FHA.summary: FHA's Minimum Property Requirements say every insured home must be safe, sound and secure. The FHA appraiser checks this on site as the lender's representative and conditions the appraisal on any required repairs (II.A.3.a.ii; appraiser standards in II.D.3). These are the rules in effect in Handbook 4000.1 Update 18 (published 8/12/2026). HUD posted a proposed MPR rewrite for comment in September 2026, but it was not final as of 2026-11-21.

VA.name: VA Home Loan Guaranty
VA.summary: VA's Minimum Property Requirements make sure a home is safe, structurally sound and sanitary before VA guarantees the loan (Ch.12 Topic 1). VA fee appraisers recommend repairs, not inspections. This version applies to appraisals ordered after May 1, 2026 (Change 46, 2/27/2026), which removed the non-vented heater, detached-improvement and radon provisions and renumbered Topics 34-43.

USDA.name: USDA Rural Development (Single Family Housing Guaranteed Loan Program)
USDA.handbook: HB-1-3555, Chapter 12 (Property and Appraisal Requirements) and Chapter 13 (Special Property Types)
USDA.summary: USDA requires an existing dwelling to meet the current minimum property requirements of HUD Handbook 4000.1, and a qualified appraiser may certify that it does (HB-1-3555 12.9(A)). USDA adds its own rules for well water testing and septic evaluations (12.6), environmental hazards and flood zones (12.10), and manufactured homes (Ch.13). New construction must instead meet ICC/IECC codes and USDA's inspection and warranty rules (12.9(B)).

wdo.FHA: For existing homes, a termite or wood-destroying insect inspection is required only when the appraiser sees evidence of infestation or prior treatment, or is notified of one. The appraisal is then made subject to inspection by a qualified pest control specialist, and the lender must get the inspection plus proof of any treatment before approving the property (HUD 4000.1 II.D.3.m.iii; II.A.3.a.ii(Q)). Soil poisoning is an unacceptable treatment unless the water supply is protected (II.A.3.a.ii(Q)). For new construction, a builder's termite guarantee (form HUD-NPMA-99-A, plus NPMA-99-B if treated) is required unless the county is on HUD's Termite Treatment Exception Areas list (II.A.8.i.iv).
wdo.VA: A wood-destroying insect report is required (1) whenever infestation or damage is apparent, with all damage repaired (M26-7 Ch.12 Topic 33a), and (2) on every origination appraisal in areas rated 'very heavy' or 'moderate to heavy' on the Termite Infestation Probability Map (Topic 33b). VA's Local Requirements page lists the affected states (last updated 7/11/2025): entire-state requirement in AL, AZ, AR, CA, CT, DE, DC, FL, GA, HI, IL, IN, KS, KY, LA, MD, MA, MS, MO, NJ, NM, NC, OH, OK, RI, SC, TN, TX, VA, WV and the territories; certain counties only in CO, IA, NE, NV, NY, PA, UT and WI. In unlisted states, no report is needed unless the appraisal notes a problem. High-rise condo units are exempt, and side-by-side condo or townhome units in required zones need a report unless the HOA shows evidence of treatment (Topic 33e).
wdo.USDA: A termite or pest inspection is required when the lender, appraiser, inspector or state law requires one to confirm the property is free of active infestation (HB-1-3555 12.9(A)). Because USDA adopts HUD 4000.1 for existing dwellings, FHA's rule also applies: evidence of infestation means inspection and treatment.

ws.FHA: Well water must meet local or state health standards, or EPA standards (40 CFR 141-142) where there are none. A well water test is required for new construction, when the appraiser reports a well or water deficiency, when the water is known to be unsafe, or when the home is near dumps, landfills, industrial sites or farms that use pesticides (HUD 4000.1 II.A.3.a.ii(N)(2)(a)). The appraiser must also require a test or inspection for nearby intensive agriculture, mining or drilling, or a dump, gas station or dry cleaner within a quarter mile, among other triggers (II.D.3.o.v(C)). A disinterested third party must collect and test the sample, and the report may be no more than 180 days old at disbursement (II.A.3.a.ii(N)(2)(b)). Minimum distances for existing construction: 10 ft from the property line, 50 ft from the septic tank and 100 ft from the drain field (75 ft if local authority allows); greater local distances prevail. Existing wells must deliver at least 3 gpm, and new ones 5 gpm over four hours (II.A.3.a.ii(N)(2)(a); 24 CFR 200.926d(f)). Wells need a pressure tank of at least 42 gallons or equivalent (II.D.3.o.v(C)). Septic systems must dispose of waste without nuisance or health hazard, and an inspection is required if there are signs of failure. A failed system must be connected to available public sewer or repaired or replaced to health department standards (II.D.3.p; II.A.3.a.ii(P)).
ws.VA: Well water must meet the local health authority's requirements, or EPA guidelines if there are none, and a disinterested third party must collect and test the sample (M26-7 Ch.12 Topic 16a-b). Results are valid for 90 days unless the local authority says otherwise (Topic 16f). The appraiser must know local well-to-pollution-source distances but is not required to measure them, and Chapter 12 states no numeric setbacks (Topic 16e). Dug wells, cisterns, hauled water, chlorinators, springs, lakes, rivers, sand-point or artesian wells and rainwater catchment require the Veteran's written acknowledgment (Topic 16c). A septic system must dispose of all waste in a sanitary manner, and health authority approval is required for proposed construction, when the appraiser notes a problem, or where soils have known percolation problems (Topic 17a, 17c). Connection to public water or sewer is required where the local authority mandates it (Topic 15g).
ws.USDA: Every individual private well needs a water quality test by the local health authority or a state-certified lab, no more than 180 days old at closing, meeting state or local standards or EPA maximum contaminant levels (HB-1-3555 12.6(A)(1)). The distance between the well and the septic system must be measured and must meet HUD 4000.1 or be acceptable to the local or state health authority (12.6(A)(1); 12.6(B)(1)). The lender must get a septic evaluation, which may come from a qualified appraiser certifying the home meets HUD 4000.1, a health authority, a licensed septic professional or a qualified home inspector. The system must show no evidence of failure and must sit entirely on the property, or on recorded easements (12.6(B)(1)). In flood zones, homes on septic need a water supply protected from cross-contamination (12.10(B)).

avi: HUD form HUD-92564-CN, 'For Your Protection: Get a Home Inspection' (rev. 02/09/2023), states that an appraisal estimates the home's value for the lender and does not replace a home inspection. FHA does not guarantee the value or condition of the home and cannot lend money for repairs or buy the home back if problems surface after closing.

FHA does not perform home inspections; one only happens if the buyer arranges and pays for it (HUD-92564-CN). FHA lenders must give the form to prospective buyers at first contact (HUD 4000.1 II.A.1.a.ii(A)(3)), and USDA lenders must also provide it and keep evidence in the loan file (HB-1-3555 12.9(A)).

VA's Lenders Handbook says an appraisal is not a home inspection: the fee appraiser does not perform operational checks of mechanical systems or appliances and estimates value to make sure it supports the loan (M26-7 Ch.12 Topic 1b). The Notice of Value issued to the Veteran recommends getting a home inspection (Topic 1g).

Appraisers observe only readily accessible, readily observable conditions. For example, FHA appraisers are not required to disturb insulation, move items or put tools inside the electrical panel (HUD 4000.1 II.D.3.f.ii, II.D.3.j-l), VA appraisers do not have to climb onto roofs or into attics (M26-7 Ch.12 Topics 26c, 27a), and an FHA appraiser's pest observation 'is not required to be at the same level as a qualified pest control specialist' (II.D.3.m.iii).

USDA requires lenders to encourage buyers to get a detailed home inspection independent of the appraisal (HB-1-3555 12.9(A)), and HUD's form recommends radon testing and asking the inspector about mold, water quality, asbestos, lead paint and pests (HUD-92564-CN).

items.text: The roof covering must keep moisture out and offer reasonable future utility, durability and economy of maintenance.
The roof must have at least two years of remaining physical life; if less, the FHA appraisal is made subject to inspection by a professional roofer.
When a defective roof with three or more layers of shingles must be replaced, all old shingles must be removed first.
The foundation and structure must be sound and serviceable for the life of the mortgage; observed structural problems trigger a repair or an inspection.
Defects that impair safety, sanitation or structural soundness (such as leaks, decay, excessive dampness, active settlement or poor workmanship) must be fixed before the loan can close.
The basement must be free of dampness, wetness and obvious structural problems that could affect occupant health or the soundness of the structure.
There must be no visibly frayed or exposed electrical wiring anywhere in the home, garage or basement.

The electrical service must be adequate for lighting and the home's normal appliances and equipment; FHA appraisers operate a sample of switches, fixtures and receptacles and report inadequate amperage or panel size.
Each living unit needs a continuous supply of safe, potable water under adequate pressure, plus domestic hot water.
Each living unit needs at least one bathroom (toilet, sink and tub or shower) and a kitchen area with a sink with running water and a stove hookup.
The plumbing must deliver water pressure and flow and remove waste, with no foul odors or readily observable leaks or damage under fixtures.
The water heater must have a temperature and pressure-relief valve with discharge piping that safely diverts escaping steam or hot water.

Private well water must meet local or state health standards (EPA drinking-water standards if none), and any required water sample must be collected and tested by a disinterested third party, never the buyer or seller.

For existing homes, an FHA well must be at least 10 ft from the property line, 50 ft from the septic tank and 100 ft from the drain field (75 ft if local rules allow), or farther where local rules require.
Water from a mechanical chlorinator, spring, lake, river, sand-point well or artesian well makes a property ineligible for FHA; VA instead requires the Veteran's signed acknowledgment.
A shared well needs a recorded, binding well-sharing agreement with a maintenance easement; FHA and USDA also require a shut-off valve for each dwelling and a limit of four homes.
An onsite septic system must dispose of all household waste without creating a nuisance or health hazard; visible signs of failure trigger an inspection or repair.

A permanently installed heating system must automatically keep the home at 50°F or higher (FHA: in living areas and in areas with freeze-prone components; VA: in areas with plumbing), using a fuel that is readily available locally.
Heating and other mechanical systems must be safe to operate and protected from destructive elements; FHA also requires reasonable future utility and adequate capacity.
Central air conditioning is not required, but if it is installed it must work; FHA appraisers report a cost to cure, and VA requires repair by a licensed HVAC contractor.
The property must be free of known environmental and safety hazards that threaten occupant health, structural soundness or normal use of the property.
Security bars on bedroom windows must be reported (FHA), and VA requires a quick-release on at least one window per bedroom unless the bedroom has an exterior door.
A room that cannot provide emergency entry and exit cannot be counted as a bedroom on an FHA appraisal.
A pool with unstable sides or structural problems must be repaired or filled in under local rules, and pools must meet local ordinances, including securing requirements.

The home needs safe pedestrian access and all-weather vehicle access from a public street, or from a private road protected by a permanent recorded easement (VA also requires an HOA or joint maintenance agreement).
The lot must be graded so that water drains away from the foundation without ponding next to the house.
Homes in a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area need flood insurance, and VA will not lend in an SFHA where flood insurance is not available.
High-voltage transmission lines may not pass directly over the house, other structures or a pool (FHA), and no part of the house may sit in a transmission-line easement (VA).

A property line within 300 ft of an aboveground tank of more than 1,000 gallons of flammable or explosive material makes the home FHA-ineligible; VA requires disclosure and the Veteran's signed acknowledgment.
Utilities must be independent for each living unit; in a 2-4 unit building, shared services need separate shut-offs for each unit.

FHA appraisers operate the plumbing, heating and electrical systems, so utilities should be on; if they are off, the appraisal is made subject to reobservation (VA appraisers do not operate the systems).
Where public water or sewer is available (FHA: at reasonable cost; VA: when the local authority mandates connection), the home must be connected.
Visible evidence of wood-destroying insects, fungus or dry rot (for FHA, including prior treatment) requires a pest inspection, with any treatment and damage repairs completed.
A wood-destroying insect report is required for VA loans in areas with 'very heavy' or 'moderate to heavy' termite probability, regardless of observed damage.

In homes built before 1978, all cracking, scaling, chipping, peeling or loose paint is presumed to be lead-based and must be repaired lead-safely; FHA covers interior, exterior and outbuilding surfaces.
For homes built in 1978 or later, FHA requires repair of defective exterior paint that exposes the surface to the elements; VA now treats such paint as normally cosmetic.
Safely accessible attics are viewed, and deficiencies such as water-stained ceilings, poor ventilation or a mold smell lead to a repair or inspection condition.
The crawl space must be accessible, clear of debris and properly vented, and excessive dampness or standing water must be corrected.

A manufactured home must be built to HUD's Manufactured Home Construction and Safety Standards (on or after June 15, 1976) and carry the HUD certification label and data plate; a missing label needs an IBTS verification letter.
USDA will only guarantee an existing manufactured home made within 20 years of closing and never installed on another site, or a new unit made within 12 months of closing.

The home must sit on a permanent foundation; FHA and USDA require compliance with HUD's Permanent Foundations Guide for Manufactured Housing, certified for FHA by a state-licensed engineer or architect.
A manufactured home must have at least 400 sq ft of floor area (VA: 700 sq ft for a double-wide).
The towing hitch and running gear must be removed.
The space beneath the home must be fully enclosed by a continuous, ventilated perimeter wall or skirting that is permanently attached.

Additions or structural changes require inspection by the state manufactured-housing agency or a licensed structural engineer (FHA), and USDA prohibits alterations other than porches or decks built to engineered designs and approved by code officials.
